items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — There's something both new and classic about Versailles... perhaps because it's from the '90s, but this French quartet could sound both symphonic and rock... with a touch of music hall, and beyond the very well-executed vocals in their original French, the instrumental sections were surprising, maintaining the intrigue without revealing the direction they would take. A certain urgency in the basic, somewhat mellow rock parts evaporated when passages typical of space rock arrived, with impressive Genesis-esque keyboard solos, all in the first of the album's three suites, Hybridite. Then came a distinctly Floydian section, with the bass and cosmic guitar alternating with the flute of Guillaume de la Piliere, their guitarist and singer.Brothers Benoit and Oliver de Gency on drums and bass respectively, along with Alain de Lille on keyboards, formed the core of this group that would produce three symphonic gems, the first of which is Don Giovanni. Erre au fil des �res, the second track, shines with mellotron and harpsichord, and the magnificent voice of Guillaume de la Piliere, who knows when to be dark and prophetic, or hopeful and celestial at other times. The complex guitar arrangements, sounding like cellos, and plucked bass lines with the mellotron in the background help create that dreamlike atmosphere, enhanced by the occasional whisper, the nuances of French chanson that run through your veins. Suddenly, a piano and flute emerge, and we see that there are ideas... there are melodies, there is execution, but there is also feeling, there is personality.Any trace of roughness seems to have been left in the past at this point, and complex arrangements and sophisticated sounds, as if we were at court, with guitars that ascend while the drums and keyboard accompany until the dramatic climax with the organ...which gives way to Don Giovanni, the central piece.There's a looseness in the bass, which at times gives the development a feel reminiscent of Yes, but when we least expect it, there's an almost chamber-like moment with flute and mellotron, with Guillaume singing and more elements that achieve that hybrid of cabaret and opera, in a context that then returns to the rock that ranges from King Crimson to Rush. Plus Alain de Lille's piano, which completely changes the mood, becoming classical in a fugue and leaving no symphonic corner unexplored... but feeling that they were not paying homage to anyone, but rather an original work, dedicated to Don Giovanni, whose imprint resonates deeply when the guitar is left alone and the whole band explodes for the grand finale.By the time we hear Subtiles D�licatesses...first solo with the harpsichord and then rocking out...Guillaume de la Piliere has become a new classic in his own right. Because he sings with such boldness, provocatively, with deep, high notes, and then the sharp guitar takes over...and then the other side with the harpsichord, with which he sings in unison.I'm not a fan of neo-progressive bands; I often demand originality from them and not copies of the classics of the past. That's why I usually stick to a few Norwegian ones, but this one really has something for me. There are influences, but "the tree doesn't obscure the forest," so to speak.Memoires D'H�catombes holds surprises, in addition to instrumental parts with pyrotechnic solos, then there will be variations with synthesizer solos in the style of Gong, of space rock...and a very operatic soprano voice floating in space only sustained by a rope, a thin rope of mellotron...to then close with bass and keyboard like a captivating whirlwind.Drama transcribes that operatic tension exposed throughout the album, with layers of keyboards like closing a curtain...a mantle of sober recollection after the exposed artificial lights, keys that like strings ascend...until they vanish in an echo that promises continuation.
items._cn_summary: 法国交响前卫摇滚乐队Versailles于1992年发行的专辑《Don Giovanni》，融合了交响摇滚、法国香颂、空间摇滚与古典元素。评论详细描述了专辑三段式结构与复杂的编曲手法，键盘手Alain de Lille的古典钢琴技法与赋格段落成为亮点。吉他手Guillaume de la Piolière的人声表现突出，兼具阴暗预言感与希望光芒。作为法语演唱的交响前卫作品，其融合了歌剧、卡巴莱与King Crimson、Rush等摇滚风格，展现出独特的法国文化视角。复杂的器乐编排与多层风格的交织体现了创作者的个人特色，属于交响前卫摇滚领域中具有原创性的作品。

items.body: Ljubljana EBM and electronic rock act Borghesia will see their 1989 album “Resistance” reissued by Matrix Music Arhiv (MMA) on 26 June 2026. The release is available across four formats: a limited purple-and-white double vinyl, a black double vinyl, a double CD, and a limited-edition cassette of 100 copies. The double vinyl and double CD editions include a bonus live album, “Dal Vivo a El Paso”, recorded in Torino, Italy in December 1988. The album has been remastered for this release. The original album occupies LP1/CD1 across all formats. Tracks are: “Theme One (Resistance Mix)”, “Message”, “If”, “Konflikt (Conflict)”, “October”, “Rumours”, “Young Prisoners”, “Discipline”, “Mali Čovek (The Little Man)”, “PIAS”, “Police Hour”, and “More Resistance”. The bonus live recording, “Dal Vivo a El Paso” – the title translates from Italian as “Live at El Paso” – makes up LP2/CD2 on the double vinyl and double CD editions. The recording was made during a European tour stop in Torino in December 1988 featuring very different, raw and at times ‘dubbed up’ versions of the band’s early tracks. Tracks are: “Hunters (Lovci)”, “Am I?”, “Sentenced To Death (Na smrtno kazen)”, “Who Turned Off the Light? (Kdo je ugasnil luč?)”, “Him (On)”, “Naked Lunch (Pasto nudo)”, “So Young (Tako mladi)”, “Rugged City (Ogolelo mesto)”, “Mud (Blato)”, and “Naked, Uniformed, Dead (Goli, uniformirani, mrtvi)”. The cassette edition, limited to 100 copies on purple MusiCassette, contains the LP1/CD1 tracks only. About the original ‘Resistance’ release Borghesia’s “Resistance” was first released in 1989 on Play It Again Sam (PIAS) in Europe, Wax Trax in the US, and Jugoton in Yugoslavia. It was among a sequence of Borghesia releases on PIAS between 1987 and 1991, which were also licensed to Wax Trax in the US and Canada. The album’s production sounded like it was created in a bunker, using stolen military equipment and synthesisers. Matrix Music Arhiv connects the reissue to current political conditions: “The dark clouds of violence are already looming over Europe, they’ve never really left the Middle East, and the levers of power and capital ever so louder, not even covertly at all incite: war, war, war!” Side-Line published a Click Interview with Borghesia in March 2019, in which Aldo Ivančič discussed the band’s history, their place in EBM’s early period, and the 2018 album “Proti Kapitulaciji” on Moonlee Records. About Borghesia Borghesia was formed in Ljubljana, Yugoslavia (now Slovenia) in 1982 by Dario Seraval (vocals, programming) and Aldo Ivančič (drums, programming), along with video artists Zemira Alajbegović, Neven Korda, and Goran Devide. The project grew out of the alternative theatre groups Theatre FV-112/15 and Teater Performans. Early releases appeared on the Slovenian label Zalozba FV and the Italian label Materiali Sonori: “Ljubav je hladnija od smrti” (1985) and “Their Laws, Our Lives” (1986). From 1987 the band issued a series of records on PIAS: “No Hope, No Fear” (1987), “Escorts and Models” (1988), the single “Naked, Uniformed, Dead” (1988), and “Resistance” (1989). PIAS releases were licensed to Wax Trax in the US and Canada. Borghesia and Laibach both appeared on “Trans Slovenia Express”, a compilation released on Mute Records in 1994. Following “Resistance”, the band released “Message” (PIAS, 1990), “4×12” (Blind Dog Records, 1991), and “Dreamers in Colour” (PIAS, 1992). The band halted all of its activity in 1995 with “Pro Choice” on Zalozba FV. The band resumed activity in 2009 and a retrospective double CD, “20th Century – Selected Works”, appeared on FV Music the same year. “And Man Created God” was released on Metropolis Records in 2014. A year later Dario Seraval appeared as a guest vocalist on dreDDup’s track “Etika” for the Side-Line free compilation “Face the Beat: Session 2”. Face The Beat: Session 2 by dreDDup “Proti Kapitulaciji” followed on Moonlee Records in 2018, and “Un Chant d’Amour” appeared on Final Muzik in 2021. The current touring lineup includes Irena Tomažin and Jelena Rusjan (vocals) and Andrej Mazi (guitar) alongside core members Seraval and Ivančič. The MMA reissue of “Resistance” is released on 26 June 2026.

items.body: DeForrest Brown Jr's final release under the moniker is out in July Speaker Music, the alias of producer and writer DeForrest Brown Jr., is to release his final album under the alias this summer. Titled Synoptic Audio, it draws to a close a partnership with Planet Mu that started in 2019 with Of Desire, Longing, and has also encompassed two further LPs: 2020's Black Nationalist Sonic Weaponry and 2023's Techxodus. items.body: When considering the title, one might imagine the answer as “sound,” as the post-rock collective Hanry, as the album, or all three. Defined as a “meditation on emergence,” What Came From Silence is a celebration of music and a coming-out party for the French band, who has released a series of EPs and singles leading up to this full-length debut. The core trio becomes a quintet for this release, the typical post-rock setup enhanced by piano, cello and electronics. In deference to the title, the set starts with “Noise Drowns Out,” which rises from silence rather than attacking; this smooth entry allows the theme of emergence to take hold. The background sheen is like a drone upon which the percussion – both organic and inorganic – begins to dance, after which the guitars are slowly mixed in like eggs to a cake. The first big post-rock moment arrives at 2:59 of this opening piece, as the instruments take a big breath, hold it for a moment, and then let it out, producing a magnetic burst that has already been fairly compared to Explosions in the Sky. Many such moments will dot the album, which flows beautifully from beginning to end. The final crunchy seconds cede space to one last piano note, which serves as a reminder: noise may drown out silence, but silence can also drown out noise. Bass-driven single “Aurora” follows, working perfectly in context, but demonstrating why the full album is more important than the singles. Removed from such context, the track is appealing, yet unlike the opening piece, its calming melodies contain only minor eruptions. What Came From Silence is far more than the sum of its parts, and deserves to be heard as a whole. This way, one may view “Aurora” as the trough from which “Dustwake” rises, bearing an increasing dramatic tension. In like fashion, the contrast between sedate piano and agitated electronics in the next piece yields to a surprising sweetness as the elements are reconciled and topple into a happy tempo surge. By the end of “Time’s Collapsing,” the album has settled into a literal rhythm. Every sound has found its place, and the collective seems jubilant. The idea of time collapsing becomes less of an end-of-the-world scenario as the sensation of losing track of time. This all culminates in the nine-minute closer, “Phantom Rush,” the band flexes its muscles to produce a two-part anthem, their longest piece to date. Hearkening back to “Noise Drowns Out,” the track produces a bookend moment at 1:39, increasing one’s appreciation of the album as a whole; the pause and attack is repeated exactly two minutes later, to even greater heights. A train track timbre connects both parts, the second borrowing from modern composition to end in elegant fashion. Perhaps thanks to the rigors of touring and the experience of producing shorter sets, Hanry has produced a debut that is head and shoulders over many of its post-rock peers. What Came From Silence is subtle enough to distort time, but specific enough to demand it; as soon as the album is over, one wants to hear it again. (Richard Allen)
items._cn_summary: 这是一张法国后摇滚乐队的首张专辑，乐队三重奏扩展为五重奏，融入钢琴、大提琴与电子元素。专辑以「沉默中浮现」为主题开场，从静音中逐渐加入打击乐、吉他与器乐层次，编排精细且有戏剧张力。评论提到与Explosions in the Sky的比较，九分钟长曲《Phantom Rush》展现乐队对专辑形式完整性的追求。音乐性扎实，融合了后摇滚、电子与新古典元素，但整体仍在后摇滚框架内，缺乏更激进的实验性探索。对于偏好实验/前卫与电子的用户而言，这张专辑在风格匹配度上属于中等偏上水平，是有质感的独立发行，但在创新程度上未能达到用户口味的更高期待。

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — By the mid-1970s the city of Barcelona, Spain was bustling with creative young musicians discoveringthe exciting new world of progressive sounds echoing from neighboring lands all with a sense ofapprehension given Spain was under the dictatorship of Franco during the prog and fusion peak yearsof the early 1970s and while the nation would go gangsbuster following the collapse of the regime in1975, certain determined bands got a head start finding ways to coexist within the framework of thetotalitarian regime. One such act was COMPANYIA EL�CTRICA DHARMA that emerged from the Santsneighborhood of Gaudi's architectural palette city. This band was formed by the three Fortunybrothers: Esteve (guitar), Josep (drums) and Joan (soprano saxophone) and once they incorporatedbassist Carles Vidal and keyboardist Jordi Soley into the team, a new band was born.The brothers initially played together as Els Llums (The Lights) as far back as 1967 and retainedmuch of the psychedelic 60s with their new baby however this band was diving headfirst into theprogressive rock era and by the time the band got to its debut release DIUMENGE (Sunday) in 1975 ithad become a fully developed jazz fusion band with influences from Miles Davis, The Weather Report,John McLaughlin, Wayne Shorter and others melding into the world of local Catalonian traditionalsounds infused with a Mediterranean charm all its own. An all instrumental affair, this debutcaptured the relaxed regional vibe and more on the subdued mellow side of the fusion equationespecially when compared to the rowdy technical free-for-all of contemporaries like M�sica Urbana orOrquestra Mirasol both of whom the band had the honor of playing with.Another feature that C.E.D. captured was the use of Spanish ethnic music outside the Cataloniaplaybook and while not a primarily flavoring, the Andalusian flamenco sounds do find their way intothe mix only primarily as subtle rhythmic undertones. The album is more on the accessible side ofthe jazz fusion spectrum with funk-infused grooves often serving as the rhythmic backbone forelectric guitar and keyboard trade offs that the opening "Fesomies Urbanes" sets the stage alongwith more moments of total chill out such as on the two part "L'harmoniosa Simfonia d'un cos." Thisparticular track showcases the strong softer side of The Weather Report with synthesized vibraphonekeys in cahoots with a sultry sax presence and a rather unhurried bass and percussion rhythmicdrive. Perhaps a little too light for some as a fusion album as the band never really dishes out any wildantics and the steadfast delivery system keeps it in the safe warm and fuzzy zone but despite themore Weather Report end of the fusion dial, COMPANYIA EL�CTRICA DHARMA's remains a competent andcaptivating piece of Catalonian jazz fusion that must be remembered was released in early 1975before Franco's death therefore the band was compelled to play it safe. This is one of the few bandsfrom the Spanish 70s prog scene that actually found international success and has existed in oneshape or form to the present era although only saxophonist Joan Fortuny is the only founding memberto survive and carry the mantle. For my tastes not the highlight of Spanish fusion but certainly anessential edition when navigating the top tier acts of the era.
items._cn_summary: 1975年西班牙巴塞罗那的爵士融合乐队C.E.D.由三兄弟组成，融合了Miles Davis、Weather Report等爵士摇滚影响与加泰罗尼亚地中海传统。专辑为纯器乐作品，风格偏向Weather Report柔和一面，弗拉门戈元素仅作为微妙节奏铺垫。作品整体在安全温暖的氛围中展开， funk风格groove与电吉他、键盘对话，萨克斯与合成器 vibraphone 构建慵懒氛围。因处于弗朗哥独裁末期，乐队选择较为保守的演奏方式，缺乏激进的即兴实验。虽然在爵士融合框架内具有地域文化特色，但整体创新性有限，适合偏好学院派爵士且对西班牙地区融合感兴趣的用户。

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — Weltschmerz by Doc W'r Mirran has some good interesting use of drone, noise and electronics from the German trio, but it does go into some repetitive Merzbow territory at times. While they have made some interesting music in the past, this is one of their noisyest projects to date. Creative at times, especially with vocal samples, it does hold some interesting moments throughout, especially with some of the more extreme moments. But it is a tad too long with a good bit of repetition. I'd give this a low to mid 6 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is Trunt.

items.body: Review by The Progolyte — I've already reviewed Latte E Miele's debut record on here, and I generally enjoyed it quite a bit. So, when I heard there was a reworking of the record over four decades later that was even better, I knew I had to check it out. This was their next project after the reunion in the late 2000s brought their first studio album in over thirty years (not counting the archival release of Vampyrs) and is supposedly their all-time best according to ProgArchives. Usually, I tend to stay away from re-recordings of albums by bands (for example, I only listened to PFM's English versions of their records recently), but with such remarkable ratings and reviews, I decided to see how good it really was. After going through it a few times, I think I still view their debut as my favorite album by theirs, but this one was still pretty strong. A little slow, admittedly, but well written and swelling with that antique feel that I love about more modern progressive rock. Moving on, one of the things I really thought was cool was that not only was the original lineup still here, but some of the various narrators on here are from other Italian bands that I adore (for example, one of my favorites being Lino Vairetti of Osanna). The album has a whopping 19 songs on it, each of which being only a few minutes long. The first few songs didn't leave much of an impression on me, being more focused and building emotional support for what would come later on the record. I felt like the real deal truly began with the third track, Ultima Cena, which is more energized and fun with some quirky keyboards and steady drumming going more along a sort of "jam" feel at points. I would say Il Pane e il Sangue dell'Alleanza and Getzemani were probably the strongest songs on the album and contain the most depth and technicality. They're very good examples of the modern Rock Progressivo Italiano scene and have a lot of different sections, each offering their own interesting mix of chamber music, folk, classical music, and, of course, progressive rock. This opening set of tracks was the main highlight of the record, and to me, the rest just repeat this formula and never really branch off into something that can catch my ear again. It may be consistent in terms of quality, but it's lacking a kick that I like in my progressive rock. The majority of the pieces are also just a little too short and could've been extended to make more of an impact on my overall view on the music here, as the music here seems to move too fast. Some of the ones that break free of this are the gloomier and heavier atmospheres of Il Rinnegamento di Pietro and Il Prezzo del Sangue, which also have the benefit of being longer. In the latter half of the album, the main highlights were Toccata Per Organo and Come un Ruscello Che, as the rest of the songs were all simply good but nothing truly amazing. The first of those two was a very well put-together organ solo in the style of something similar to Emerson, Lake, and Palmer's Three Fates composition, and the second, Come un Ruscello Che, serves as the finale to the album and wraps it up nicely and in a strong manner. Something I did like about some of these later songs, however, was their use as medleys, which built up more suspense and drama for the finale in longer-format atmospheric music that congregates into the next song rather than stopping the flow. In conclusion, while not a full-on masterpiece of modern Rock Progressivo Italiano, Latte E Miele still definitely puts on a great performance. The music here is wonderful and full of depth, and while lacking a last push of power and invigorated enthusiasm, it still has an overall epic feel to it that fits its progressive rock nature. I'm awarding this album a low 4/5, but I may be returning to it in the future for a reevaluation.
items._cn_summary: 这张《Passio Secundum Mattheum》是意大利前卫摇滚乐队Latte E Miele于2014年发行的重录专辑，收录于《The Complete Work》合集中。专辑共19首曲目，延续了意大利前卫摇滚融合古典、室内乐和民谣的传统风格。评论者指出其融合了chamber music、folk、古典音乐与前卫摇滚元素，具有浓郁的古朴气息。专辑亮点集中于中段曲目如《Ultima Cena》《Il Pane e il Sangue dell'Alleanza》等，展现了乐队在编曲上的技术性和情绪张力。然而评论者认为整体节奏偏慢，曲目过于短促缺乏延展性，后半部分重复套路未能提供更多惊喜。对于偏好实验性和创新性的听众而言，这张专辑在意大利前卫摇滚范畴内编曲扎实、跨流派融合自然，但在实验锐度和前卫突破上相对保守，更接近传统意义上的融合艺术摇滚而非激进实验。

items.body: Es gibt Musik, die braucht Nebel, einen dunklen und verschwitzten Club, gepaart mit dieser leichten Anspannung in der Luft, um sich wahrlich entfalten zu können. Wenn aber Mathias Modica aka Kapote an den Decks beginnt, spielt das alles keine Rolle mehr. Der Toy Tonics-Chef, Produzent und DJ kuratiert Tracks, die sich nicht nach dem kalten Berliner Beton anfühlen. Schließt man die Augen, könnte man fast meinen, man sitze auf dem Beifahrersitz eines Cabrios an einem warmen Sommertag, während man italienische Serpentinen herunterfährt, dem Meer entgegen. Um zu verstehen, was den Sound von Kapote ausmacht, lohnt sich ein Blick zurück in die Vergangenheit, zu seinem früheren Ich. Über anderthalb Jahrzehnte prägte Modica als Munk und Kopf des legendären Münchner Labels Gomma Records die europäische Clubkultur. Munks Ansatz war sowohl eklektisch als auch tief verwurzelt im Post-Punk, No-Wave und Indie-Disco. Fast wie das Gegenstück steht Kapote für Wärme, lebendigen Sound, slappende Bässe und hypnotische Grooves, die aus einer Mischung aus Detroiter Elektro-Funk, New Yorker Garage-House und Chicago House hervorgehen. Luftiges Urgestein Dass dieser Sound so tief atmet, liegt auch an Modicas kollektivem Geist. Im Laufe seiner Karriere kollaborierte er mit einer wahnsinnig großen Riege an visionären Künstler:innen von James Murphy über Peaches bis hin zu WhoMadeWho. Nach seinem Umzug in die Hauptstadt hat er sich längst in der Berliner House-Szene etabliert. Als Mastermind hinter Toy Tonics, welches er gemeinsam mit Freunden gründete, formt er von hier aus ein globales Netzwerk. Auch in seinem Guest Mix schafft Kapote einen Raum, der luftig leicht ist. Mittels Einflüssen aus Italo-Disco und Disco-House-Grooves demonstriert er bestens das Zusammenspiel seiner typischen gestalterischen Gewerke. Statt steriler Monotonie rollen Rhythmen unaufhaltsam vorwärts, während organische Vocal-Loops und jazzige Percussions perfekt ineinandergreifen. According to a press release, it's a concept album that is set in the year 2097, and imagines a mass human exodus from Earth to the Vega star system which is situated 25.3 light-years away. items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — Explorers Club is one of the most exciting prog supergroups of the 90s. This Magna Carta project isheaded and masterminded by Trent Gardner, keyboard player and songwriter for Magellan, who is herejoined by John Petrucci on guitars, Billy Sheehan on bass guitar, and Terry Bozzio on drums,together with four different vocalists, among which the names of James LaBrie and D. C. Cooper makea serious impression. Additionally, the supergroup's debut album features contributions from DerekSherinian (keyboards), Wayne Gardner (guitars), Steve Howe (acoustic guitar), and James Murphy(guitars). Composed by Trent Gardner, 'Age of Impact', as goes the title of this 1998 album, is abold musical odyssey that for me represents one of the most successful collaborations in modernprogressive rock. The music of Explorers Club is a daring marriage of heavy but melodic neo-prog andtechnical prog metal, featuring lost of shredding and mind-bending soloing, complex arrangements andextended instrumental sections, polyrhythms, and a few truly experimental bits.I am certain that this album was conceived as one continuous piece of music, and while the albumtrack list features five distinct compositions, the former are actually connected and flow into eachother almost seamlessly, giving the impression of one gargantuan composition that goes throughseveral distinct sections, but remains true to the main album theme. Opening track 'Fate Speaks'sits at sixteen minutes and happens to be one of the most technically intense pieces on here - fromthe complex opening section, which is all-instrumental, to the excellent verses that come in at alater point and the scorchingly rapid solos of John Petrucci (and James Murphy, supposedly), this isa really strong prog metal suite that features Bret Douglas as the lead vocalist. The sound is epic,bombastic, celebratory and straight up wild, and fans of LTE and Dream Theater should reallyappreciate this massive track. 'Fading Fast' then introduces a more ethereal, keyboard-driven soundas well as some world music influences, which are explored brilliantly by Trent Gardner. Third track'No Returning' revisits the heavier sounds from the beginning of the album, as this part of thesuite serves as an almost all-instrumental middle section with excellent guitars and keys, while thesole vocal part is sang by James LaBrie. 'Time Enough', which is the fourth song on the album,explores a melodramatic new age sound and features some thoughtful lyrics, which are sang by D. C.Cooper, while the closing piece 'Last Call', returns to the main theme and expands it beautifully,concluding the record with a flamboyant streak of guitar pyrotechnics, occupying a good chunk of the11-minute-long final composition.'Age of Impact' is a fantastic project in my view - the complexity of the compositions, thegrandiose ideas, and the excellent execution should be seen as a treat by fans of prog rock and progmetal alike. The balanced vocal work and the cohesion of the entire work are commendable, too.However, unlike LTE or Dream Theater, the music of Explorers Club manages to evoke that classic progfeeling in a beautiful way, which is why I think it is one of the most underrated heavy prog gemfrom the late 1990s.
items._cn_summary: 这是一张1998年发行的重前卫摇滚专辑，由 Magellan 键盘手 Trent Gardner 领衔的超级组合Explorers Club制作，成员包括 John Petrucci、Billy Sheehan、Terry Bozzio 等技术型音乐人。专辑采用连续的套曲结构，将重型的技术化编曲与复杂的器乐段落相结合，融入了多轨复节奏和少量实验元素，整体风格偏向重 neo-prog 与技术前卫金属的混合体。乐评指出作品在旋律和结构上较为大胆，但缺乏跨领域的深度融合，更多停留在传统前卫摇滚框架内。对于偏好实验和前卫音乐的用户而言，该专辑提供了一定的技术复杂度和编曲层次感，但与真正的实验电子、爵士或暗潮等风格存在距离，属于前卫摇滚范畴内较为保守的作品。

items.body: Review by alainPP — BRUCE SOORD's 5th album, recorded over 10 years ago, exudes a heightened dreamlike atmosphere, based on acoustic sounds, reflecting his past life like a musical epitaph."Concepcion" opens with an acoustic guitar riff, a melancholic Southern lament, an evening in Chile, a heartfelt cry for his mother giving birth. "Meet Me on the Downs" is a mid-tempo ballad with his voice as the instrument, a slow, ethereal, decrescendoing sound reminiscent of the end of a concert in Hamburg. "Pillars," with its melody etched into our musical subconscious, features a slide guitar that shines, illuminates, and opens the mind. It evokes the feeling of a Western ballad, riding these reverberating notes, rich like a cactus at sunset, where the heat makes the air vibrate. A beautiful melody dealing with excessive introspection, the quest for balance, a reference to Saint Simeon Stylite. "You Made a Promise," with its prominent, almost oppressive acoustic guitar over a pastoral choir, and a raw, crystalline vocal delivery, all in under three minutes. "Our Predicament" features lingering guitar notes and metronomic sixteenth notes amplifying the contemplative sound. The off-kilter vocals heighten the impression of a solitary lament. The electric guitar solo evokes the plaintive post-rock of KWOON, an intimate moment you wouldn't want to share with your horse at dusk. "Day of Wrath" shifts gears, repetitive from the start, reminiscent of Mariusz's work on LUNATIC SOUL. A catchy, addictive sound, and then Bruce launches into an airy, pastoral, uplifting ballad where the metronomic feel allows you to escape the torpor induced at the beginning of the album. A musical surge, ambient with an encroaching synth, the album truly takes off with this sound reminiscent of PINEAPPLE THIEF, a return to their roots. "Stared Down" returns to its primal acoustic roots, its latent intimacy lingering on post-rock undertones, reminiscent of ANATHEMA, with that famous, soaring guitar solo."Kept Me Thinking," the creaking of a chair on the side of a house in Louisiana, is the first of two long tracks; I was getting impatient. Note the contribution of Jon, a PINEAPPLE THIEF collaborator, on bass for this crescendoing track that flows like a drink in the middle of the desert. Easy melody, vocals, and a melancholic guitar worthy of Brother CAVANAGH. A track that reminds us that you don't need a whole fleet of instruments to be great. The final solo screams with joy, lets loose, and feels good; an oriental-tinged choral finale. "Ghosts in the Park" begins with a meandering acoustic guitar, the other a plaintive electric ballad typical of PINEAPPLE THIEF?old habits die hard. A suspended 1'45" intro, and you think it's over; and then, and then the air begins to move, tickling our ears, leaving us to search for the musical direction, the Oberhausen creative space. The essence of the progressive spirit is evident in the minimalist drums accompanying these radiant post-acoustic guitar notes, letting the ear wander for a long time, taking its time. The finale seems to settle at the 10-minute mark, but then comes the organic shift, a fragile, latent sound, a musical spiderweb drawing the listener into Bruce's very room, listening to him strum and hum this last fleeting, archaic, ephemeral melody.Bruce Soord has given himself up without musical artifice; emotion, restraint, intimacy, and sincerity define this stripping bare with his acoustic guitar.
items._cn_summary: 这张由布鲁斯·索德创作的专辑《Ghosts In The Park》延续了渐进摇滚的传统风格，融合了原声音乐与后摇氛围。专辑以Acoustic吉他为核心载体，通过悠远的旋律与梦境般的编曲构建出沉思性的音乐空间。评论详细描述了各曲目从忧郁的南方挽歌到西部 ballad 的多元风格，展现出渐进摇滚的叙事性与情感张力。作品在原声质朴感与渐进音乐的复杂性之间取得平衡，带有明显的Pineapple Thief与Anathema等乐队的音色印记。对于偏好实验与前卫的听众而言，这张专辑虽不具备强烈的实验性突破，但其渐进摇滚框架内的氛围营造与细腻情感表达仍具有一定审美价值。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — One might think that after an album like Scheherazade And Other Stories, and their performance at Carnegie Hall, the band might show signs of wear and tear... however, this is not evident in Novella... and Renaissance, we are talking about, the band with one of the best symphonic singers of the 70s, Annie Haslam, and, whether recognized or not, one of the best bass players in the figure of Jon Camp, as well as an excellent pianist in John Tout who tackled many genres from classical to jazz and everything in between with ease. Terence Sullivan on drums, hot on their heels in every adventure they embarked on, with those long, dreamy introductions... and Michael Dunford on acoustic guitar, because they were rarely heard with an electric guitar, although they did play with a full orchestra, which was an instrument, another member of the band, here with arrangements by Richard Hewson, which can be heard in Can You Hear Me?The bass and the orchestra lead Can You Hear Me?, taking us into a melody as delicate as it is strong, which already invites us to travel, as was its custom, through diverse lands and eras...geographies that we travel through hand in hand with Annie who sings epically until the common thread of the theme, that disruptive chorus that breaks the song, takes the scene by surprise. We can hear new elements despite it being the band's recognizable sound, and a romantic piano weaves textures while Annie changes tone. The expansive composition transitions seamlessly from one section to another and feels like a single, natural flow.The strings give way to the winds...and the trumpets highlight the clarity of Annie's voice, which rivals the oboes sustaining notes with the strings behind them, and the energetic composition picks up again...reaching the aggressiveness of a full orchestra, radically different from that of a rock group.Can the delicacy of The Sisters take us by surprise and momentarily transport us to another world? Like those children being read to from the cover, whose two versions, one for the US and one for Europe, didn't diminish the achievements of their music. The Sisters is another lesson in singing from Annie, different from her previous work, from another time... flirting with flamenco, as does her voice, and also the phrasing of the guitar and piano.The keyboards, acoustic guitar and Annie's voice followed by backing choirs make up Midas Man, almost pastoral, while The Captive Heart had the charm that in this inspired era that continued, giving life to each piano note...to each note that Annie sang, with the ideal counterpoint of the choirs of the rest of the band.Touching Once (Is So Hard to Keep) is the second most ambitious composition on the album. The piano notes foreshadow the melody that Annie will confirm, along with the rest of the band, where an almost waltz-like tango rhythm drags the strings to a false ending reminiscent of Gershwin. The orchestra then takes us by surprise, along with the band, with choirs before entering a dreamy passage of synthesizers, subtle bass and piano notes that quietly prepare the ground for a new contrast with jazzy orchestral touches, an anonymous saxophone solo that no one remembers who played in the band to this day...but which turned out fabulous, and a symphonic ending for an album rich in harmonies, sonic offerings and emotions explored...including a final coda that promises that the story will continue eternally.
items._cn_summary: Renaissance《Novella》发表于1977年，是交响前卫摇滚的典型作品。乐队核心成员包括主唱Annie Haslam、贝斯手Jon Camp、钢琴手John Tout及鼓手Terence Sullivan，并与完整交响乐团合作。专辑以宏大交响编排与摇滚乐队声部融合为特色，强调Annie卓越的声乐技巧。作品涵盖《Can You Hear Me?》《The Sisters》《Touching Once》等曲目，展现出精致的弦乐、铜管与钢琴交织，间或融入弗拉门戈元素。作为70年代交响摇滚的代表，编曲工整、层次丰富，但整体风格更接近传统前卫摇滚范畴，在实验性与当代电子/暗潮语境下创新度有限，适合对交响摇滚及声乐演绎有偏好的听众。

items.body: “Arousal” is already the third album by Italian duo Les Longs Adieux. With this new release, Federica Garenna and Frank Marrelli continue to build on their established sound while simultaneously allowing new influences and subtle evolutions to emerge. The album still breathes the spirit of the 1980s, yet this opus perhaps leans even more toward Electro-Wave territory, enriched with wonderfully vintage synthesizer textures that create a certain sense of magic. Throughout the record, a melancholic atmosphere dominates, beautifully reinforced by melodic choruses that give many of the songs an emotional depth. One particular standout is “Le Soldat De Plomb,” which incorporates a few French lyrics and is, in my opinion, by far the strongest track the duo has written so far. The song feels like a genuine gem and showcases exactly what Les Longs Adieux is capable of achieving when everything falls perfectly into place. After this high point, the album loses a bit of momentum, though it remains an enjoyable and atmospheric listen throughout, even if no additional tracks quite reach the same level. Les Longs Adieux undeniably possesses potential. They may not have fully realized it yet, but “Arousal” contains at least one truly remarkable song that is bound to resonate deeply with listeners. (Rating:7½). Listen to “Le Soldat De Plomb”: https://leslongsadieux.bandcamp.com/track/le-soldat-de-plomb

items.body: Mareux is taking his shadow-laced romance on a trek across the Atlantic. The Los Angeles darkwave artist — the project of musician and producer Aryan Ashtiani — has announced a short run of 2026 UK and European dates, beginning October 30 at Hootananny Brixton in London and continuing through Paris/Montreuil, Athens, Istanbul, and Tbilisi. Current listings place the Paris-area date at Bal Chavaux in Montreuil, the Athens date at Floyd Live Music Venue, the Istanbul date at IF Performance Hall Beşiktaş, and the Tbilisi date at Academy. The dates follow the release of last year’s Nonstop Romance, Mareux’s 2025 full-length for Revolution/Warner Records, a record that widened his smoldering synth-pop into something grander, sleeker, and more fatalistically romantic. The album includes “Blackmail,” “Radio Club,” “Wild At Heart,” “Ébène Fumé” featuring Riki, “Blue,” “Laugh Now Cry Later,” and “Snake Eyes.” Its most recent visual, the August 2025 video for “Wild At Heart,” still serves as a fitting doorway into the record’s world of bruised glamour, late-night longing, and doomed devotion. Mareux first emerged from the Los Angeles underground in the early 2010s, releasing the Decade EP in 2013 and Predestiny in 2020. Ashtiani has described early musical sparks that ranged from Eurodance heard during summers in Iran to the post-punk revival pull of Interpol and Editors; later, the cold electronic intensity of TR/ST helped steer the project toward its current darkwave direction. His best-known release remains “The Perfect Girl,” a brooding cover of The Cure’s 1987 song that became a viral streaming phenomenon in 2021. The track’s second life helped introduce Mareux’s cold, romantic synth sound to a much wider audience; its 2022 video starred Violet Chachki, and Warner’s 2023 press materials noted hundreds of millions of streams and billions of TikTok sound views around the track. ﻿ That momentum carried Mareux into larger rooms and major festivals. In 2023, he played both weekends of Coachella, released his debut album Lovers From The Past, and launched a headlining global tour with stops in Los Angeles, New York, Berlin, London, and more. He has also appeared at dark-alternative gatherings, including Darker Waves 2023 and Cruel World 2025. Before heading overseas, Mareux will appear as a special guest for AFI at an outdoor Santa Ana show on September 19 at Observatory Festival Grounds, with Kumo 99 and L.A. Witch also on the bill. See the full announced run below. Mareux 2026 Tour Dates 09/19 — Santa Ana, CA — Observatory Festival Grounds with AFI, Kumo 99, and L.A. Witch 10/30 — London, UK — Hootananny Brixton 10/31 — Paris/Montreuil, France — Bal Chavaux 11/03 — Athens, Greece — Floyd Live Music Venue 11/05 — Istanbul, Turkey — IF Performance Hall Beşiktaş 11/07 — Tbilisi, Georgia — Academy Tickets and additional information are available through Mareux’s official site and local ticketing outlets. items.body: Review by alainPP — "The Silent Architect" features an organic rhythm followed by a groove worthy of Dream Theater, a metal riff with a "Kashmir-like" feel, and a melodic battleground. Nathan's voice dazzles over a heavy prog riff reminiscent of Kamelot, for example. The guitar solo and other solos drive the frenetic rhythm and instrumental onslaught, all power metal. "Doors of Yesterday" is a melancholic ballad highlighted by Dean's piano, with a saccharine classical orchestration over a pop melody oozing emotion, its metallic riff subtly present in the background. It evokes fond memories of the 80s, a time when quality reigned supreme. "The Invisible Countdown" boasts a distinctive vocal style, a reminiscent of Vanden Plas's prog metal DNA, and a wild, heavy riff. The catchy, mainstream heavy rock melody features a sharp guitar solo and an orchestration approaching the valiant Fates Warning. The final fade-out is somewhat redundant, however. "Mr. Crazy" breaks the mold, offering the raw, frenetic, and compulsive hard rock of their earlier work, with Nathan sounding more like Aerosmith. A punk-infused track with a colossal drumbeat, perfect for some serious headbanging. "Arrow" is the second, more mainstream, mid-tempo ballad, soothing on acoustic guitar and filled with backing vocals from Nathan and Dean. The irresistible melody makes you want to sing along to the chorus, shoulders intertwined; it's 80s rock boosted by today's powerful sound."Dust & Bone" kicks off again, like a heavy machine gun, the sharp rhythm throwing debris in all directions. A near-thrash track with a raw, swirling solo and a killer rhythm section?I stand by it; punchy and explosive. "Enemy In The Garden," the fourth full-length track, features a prog-metal intro that launches Nathan's restrained vocals over guest keyboardist Matt Guillory, James Labrie's regular keyboardist. As you might have guessed, the Dream Theater influence is evident, especially with the solemn break, the pounding pads, and the melting guitar. At one point, you might think you recognize a Pink Floyd vibe, and you wouldn't be wrong. It restarts, highlighting the contrast of this seemingly effortless piece with the excellent second guitar solo. The notes are even higher, and the interplay of vocals and instruments forges the album's standout track. "Ghost Hands," the third acoustic guitar ballad, is simple, effective, gentle, and enchanting. The fragile vocals evoke goosebumps, and the obligatory guitar solo sounds even better; impressively effortless. "Left In The Fire" boasts an intro-riff worthy of Metallica; The cinematic sound brings the power of the machine-gun riff, the keyboard in the background adds the richness to highlight the best notes. It's molten prog metal, resting in its blazing furnace, with Nathan delivering a beautiful vocal performance over a terrifying, savage, tribal rhythmic foundation. A sharp break, the beauty of the acoustic sound before Dean's fiery solo forges a new musical path. The epic arrives, the arpeggio dripping down, delivering the coup de gr�ce to this track. Nick's metronomic drumming guides the finale over the vocal-guitar chord before the delicate outro, a warm acoustic guitar solo, with Nathan's performance moving to the very end.TERAMAZE is back in the saddle after their previous album; here, it's a prog metal masterpiece, blending vocals, rhythm, riffs, edgy melodies, and warm ballads.(4.25)

items.body: Review by The Progolyte — This very obscure solo artist from Rome by the name of Stefano Testa only has a single album from the seventies under his belt, but I personally think it does more than you think. It's quite pretty, lacking in terms of that overall bombastic sound that I like in most of my Italian music, but still good enough to make an impact. And with an album cover like that, you can tell there's going to be something interesting in here. I think the overall performance could've been more exciting, but the laid-back and relaxed vibes of the material sort of fit well with the more singer-songwriter-oriented music on this record, especially in the second half of the album where the songs get short. Moving on to the personnel, it's Stefano Testa on piano, rhythm guitar, and vocals, and then his band that plays with him consists of Marco Coppi on flute, Alberto Monpellio on moog, Cosimo Fabiano on bass, Ottavio Corbellini on drums, and then Portici takes care of the rest of the guitars. My favorite track on here has to be the grand and thoroughly written sixteen-minute-long suite titled Una Vita. It has various different sections stitched together into one great composition, with mainly more dramatic acoustic bits but also taking use of almost spoken word passages and steady rock rhythms. It's really strong and shows a high level of craftsmanship but is admittedly a little slow and inconsistent in parts. You could say Stefano and the band could've had more enthusiasm in their playing, and though it is strong, it feels lacking when it comes to their overall energy. The rest of the songs are all quite short and uneventful, mainly being simple melodies with limited instrumentation. You can feel like it's going somewhere, but in the end it lies stagnant and doesn't evolve in the way you'd imagine. The highlights from this section were La Ballata Di Achab/Moby Dick and Il Dio Sulla Ferrovia, which had some interesting details such as more progressive structures and sections. In conclusion, this album sort of felt like a letdown, seeing how it had a rating of 4.06 at the time of writing this, but it's still generally an okay record. A bit lacking here and there, not bringing many original ideas to the table, but still a fun one if you like your Rock Progressivo Italiano fit with a lighter and simpler tone. This record will be getting a low 3.5/5.
items._cn_summary: 这张1977年意大利进步摇滚专辑由罗马音乐人Stefano Testa创作，整体呈现较为放松的歌手-词曲作者风格。专辑最值得关注的是时长16分钟的套曲《Una Vita》，融合了戏剧性的原声段落与渐进式结构，展示了相对成熟的编曲能力。评论者指出其优势在于Craftsmanship，但整体缺乏能量与创新动力，部分歌曲显得停滞而未充分展开。考虑到用户偏好实验性与前卫性更强的作品，这类传统意大利进步摇滚虽然带有一定的渐进式元素和地方特色，但在创新性和实验性方面与用户口味匹配度有限，属于中规中矩的类型化作品。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — This version of Yes, with Jon Anderson singing so differently, so jazzy and psychedelic, already featuring Chris Squire, Bill Bruford, and Peter Banks with that variety of sounds... they would have stood out in the sea of ​​bands of the '60s even if they hadn't been the Yes we later knew. They weren't Beatles clones like so many others... and it was a different band, of course! Just listen to the acoustic ending of "Beyond and Before." And "I See You" is one of my favorite tracks... vocal harmonies in a jazzy, psychedelic context, Jon with a voice that sometimes sounded like many jazz singers at once, even Billie Holiday! Sometimes it's just the guitar and drums... and I think they were already a mature band of experienced musicians; in fact, several of them came from previous bands, and they only pale in comparison to their own future work... which was so different from what they were doing, despite the classical influences already present in Banks' solos.So what standard, what parameter to use? That of the progressive context? If so, the result would be uneven because some works were already pointing in that direction without even knowing it, while others, equally beautiful like Yesterday and Today, were more anchored in the 60s. Although that is precisely where the magic of this debut lies, its freshness, its variety...its honesty.Looking Around shows a mixed maturity, achieved in the instrumental aspect, in the execution, but not yet in the compositional aspect, where one could expect more originality in the arrangements, although the embryo of a more mature band is already present in The Yes Album years later.Harold Land displays an attempt at more complex, distinctly British composition, which, however, is light years away from the classic Yes style. Banks' guitar arrangements are impeccable, and Jon's voice is perfectly on point, emotive and epic... yet understated at the same time, which is what a song of this magnitude demands. "Every Little Thing" begins the final trio of tracks, which are also my favorites. When they stray from the script and Banks plays without following it, and Bruford follows him blindly, it's a different band, rawer, another good band with people we know, with nods to the Beatles that remain just that. And yet, the final result is uneven due to small details, such as unpredictable parts alongside others that are quite foreseeable and detract from the impact of the latter. In Sweetness you can enjoy Jon's clean and tender voice, Chris's bass, Paul Banks' guitar and Bill who could play with brushes or the edges like Brazilian bossa nova drummers, but it was still a little way off, you enjoy that previous experiment, which was definitely still a promise of what was to come...seemingly impossible to isolate oneself from the context...something that could be done with I see you.It goes without saying that Bill Bruford loves jazz... and Jon, throughout his career, has systematically returned to it like an old friend he may not see often, but whose affection remains undiminished. He has always demonstrated his attachment to the genre, whether on his second solo album, Song of Seven, or with the studio tracks on Keys to Ascension, or his collaboration with Jean-Luc Ponty a few years ago. This debut also speaks to that, and therein lies its value, beyond its level within the progressive standard.Survival has that unique magic of Swinging London...from that photo shoot with those statues in the album booklet...that makes it eternal, that never ages.
items._cn_summary: 1969年首张专辑展现了爵士与迷幻的早期融合，声乐和声在人声多重叠加中带有即兴感，Jon Anderson的唱法预示了后来的标志性风格。Peter Banks的吉他solo已融入古典影响，Bill Bruford的鼓点带有爵士即兴的痕迹。乐队虽由资深音乐家组成，展示了跨风格的融合意识，但作品成熟度参差不齐，部分曲目仍保留60年代流行摇滚的痕迹，与后来的前卫摇滚经典相比显得不够完整。评论者认为其价值在于实验性与承诺性，而非已成型的风格表达。作为早期融合作品，其实验精神与爵士元素契合用户口味，但创新程度受时代局限，整体评分适中。

items.body: Gata Galáctica wrote “Filosofía” in 2021, the first song they put together as a band in Portland, and it has opened or closed almost every set since. The track finally got recorded in 2024 at Cooper Mountain Sound with engineer Justin Robert Chase, and it comes out now as the A-side of a 7″ vinyl single, Filosofía / Manos Sucias. “Filosofía” is chicha played loud: Andrez and Manny‘s guitars cycle reverb-soaked phrases over and over while J‘s percussion refuses to let up. Dylan‘s bass and Chris‘s drums underneath keep the whole thing heavy and moving forward. The single puts two instrumental cumbias on either side of a 45, the same format that carried chicha and tropical rock across Latin America through the 1960s and 70s. Listen to “Filosofía” HERE and reserve your copy of Filosofía / Manos Sucias following THIS LINK   The post Daily Discovery: Gata Galáctica – Filosofía appeared first on Rhythm Passport.
items._cn_summary: Gata Galáctica乐队的单曲《Filosofía》是一首典型的秘鲁chicha器乐作品，吉他通过持续的reverb效果循环铺陈，打击乐维持着不间断的律动，低频部分为整体增添厚重感。该作品于2024年录制，以7寸黑胶形式独立发行，属于传统器乐cumbia范畴。音乐风格上保持了chicha与热带摇滚的经典特征，虽具有拉美地区文化特色和器乐演绎的稳定质感，但在实验性、创新性以及跨领域融合方面并未展现出显著特质，整体更接近传统世界音乐的延续性呈现。

items.body: LEVITATION will return to Austin, Texas, this September with another four-day run of psych, post-punk, darkwave, punk, metal, indie rock, and electronic music spread across the city’s Red River District, East Side venues, and beyond. The 2026 edition is set for Sept. 10 through 13, with more than 20 shows already announced and 4-day passes and single-show tickets on sale now through Levitation.fm/tix. This year’s lineup includes Bikini Kill, Molchat Doma, Angine de Poitrine, American Football, The Garden, Die Spitz, Peter Hook & The Light, Smerz, Arlo Parks, Cabaret Voltaire, Acopia, Uncle Acid & The Deadbeats, Psychedelic Porn Crumpets, Man or Astro-Man?, Los Thuthanaka, Elder, Monolord, Friko, Automatic, Sweeping Promises, DITZ, Nitzer Ebb, Tanukichan, Gibby Haynes, Melt-Banana, Pearl & The Oysters, ALI, Primitive Ring, Earth Tongue, and more. Radio/East will serve as the festival’s central hub this year, with an expanded two-stage layout, while LEVITATION’s late-night and club shows will continue across Austin at Stubb’s, Mohawk, Elysium, 29th St. Ballroom, The 13th Floor, and Central Presbyterian Church. For the post-punk and darkwave faithful, Saturday is the obvious centerpiece: Molchat Doma tops a Radio/East bill featuring Cabaret Voltaire, Peter Hook & The Light, Automatic, DITZ, Novulent, and I Speak Machine. That same night, Nitzer Ebb headlines Elysium with SINE and Curse Mackey. Thursday night brings Buzz Kull, Max Fry and Kontravoid to Elysium, while Friday’s Radio/East bill pairs Bikini Kill with Die Spitz, Gibby Haynes’ Butthole Surfers Mania, Sweeping Promises, Melt-Banana and Powerplant. Sunday’s Radio/East show still has a mystery headliner listed as “?????” alongside Uncle Acid & The Deadbeats, Psychedelic Porn Crumpets, Elder, Primitive Ring, Messa, and Earth Tongue. Additional artists, DJs, and visual artists are still to be announced. See the full schedule below. items.body: I was too young in the sixties to witness their music firsthand, yet by the time I came of age in the seventies, Jimi Hendrix had become a kind of god to me — followed later by Miles Davis and then John Coltrane . What has always astonished me is how - within the same decade - each of these towering musical geniuses forged an entirely new sound and voice from within tradition itself: honouring it, absorbing it, yet ultimately pushing beyond its boundaries until they burst free from the constraints of form altogether. Out of that rupture, they created new musical languages — languages that continue to resonate deeply with so many people and that express emotions for which words could never truly exist. Jimi Hendrix took the blues and then practised relentlessly on his guitar to expand its vocabulary, its power and its electrifying effects. This was the period of polished 2-minute pop songs, of refined vocals and backing vocals, of nicely fitting suits and the comfort of going to mom and dad in the evening. Hendrix tore it all down, yet built it up again, exposing humanity to a sonic avalanche never heard before (and rarely heard since): loud, brutal, technically brilliant, sensitive and deeply moving. Miles Davis was a little older, yet came later to my musical horizon, and I was sold immediately. My first experience was with " In A Silent Way ", and especially the title track with its steady rhythm, its hypnotic groove and its brilliant trumpet-playing is still engrained in my brain. A decade earlier, he had already changed the course history of jazz by " Kind of Blue ", a milestone then, yet when listening to it now, you wonder what all the fuzz was about, but that's primarily because it influenced all jazz after its release, as if people wondered what was so new about Picasso, who might seem somewhat conventional from today's point of view. Then " Bitches Brew ". This was it. The power, the drive, the relentless and uncompromising rhythm section, the stellar musicianship, and this "man with the horn", creating sounds also never heard before, with or without "wah wah". It defied any type of soloing heard before. It opened space, and showed that anything was possible, even chaos and noise, without restrictions with the exception of the piece's overall coherence. John Coltrane - also born in 1926 - was the third luminary. Like Davis, and in collaboration with him, they released some of the more memorable albums of the fifties with the Miles Davis Quintet: "Cookin'", "Relaxin'", "Workin'", and "Steamin'" and with the sextet later the iconic "Kind of Blue". Then he single-handedly pulled jazz out of the smoky bar rooms of the entertainment industry and turned it into Art with a capital "A": " A Love Supreme " turned music upside down. It showed something grand, a level of spirituality and personal freedom of expression rarely heard in music before, yet still compelling and mysterious despite its novel approach. Even a simple tune such as " My Favorite Things " became a mesmerising listening experience when performed by Coltrane. With " Interstellar Space ", his duo album with drummer Rashied Ali, he broke with all conventions, yet despite the negative comments from the jazz community, his technique and incredible inventiveness were beyond comparison. Despite the profound differences in their music — free blues, jazz rock, and free jazz — all three men broke with convention and revealed new ways of expressing what it means to be human. They were open to new forms, they integrated sounds from other musical styles, they were endlessly creative. Despite the many opportunities for commercial success, they kept searching, stretching their performances to lengthy and grandiose improvisations, the kind of music that would never get any radio airplay, let alone be of interest to mainstream audiences. They each struggled with drugs and addiction, but I don’t believe that alone explains the parallels between them. Even if their music was not "political" in the real sense of the word, they represented the voice of African Americans and their fight for civil rights - check Davis' " Tribute To Jack Johnson " as an example - but their music went much deeper, it was (is) the voice of more authentic feelings of anger, sadness, agony, despair, hope and transcendence than the entertainment industry could ever offer. They share a devotion to technique, not as a goal but as a means to free sound from historical constraints, and to create something more expansive, monumental, authentic, existential, spiritual, and deeply human. They transformed music. They created great art. Each possessed a sound and a voice instantly recognisable from afar, unlike anything found in music today. Miles Davis and Jimi Hendrix planned to record together. They had been preparing this for a while, and both had a show at the Isle of Wight Festival in 1970 - and by the way, it's truly amazing that Davis was invited to play at a rock festival - yet a few weeks later Hendrix died unexpectedly. Three exceptional musicians, three exceptional artists somehow met and did something similar profound for music at the same juncture in time and place. They combined creative discipline and control on the one hand, with ecstatic improvisation and raw expression on the other. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: Marcel Vallès spent three years in South America from 2012, living and playing in Chile, Argentina and Brazil before returning to his home town of Els Guiamets in Tarragona. Boas Lembranças, which translates from Portuguese as “good memories”, is what he brought back: eight guitar compositions recorded as a duo with percussionist Steve Shehan, the French-American musician of Cherokee descent who has drummed for Paul Simon, Bob Dylan and Peter Gabriel over a career spanning five decades. The two met at a festival in Morocco and the album took shape from there. Vallès recorded his parts at Estudio Guará in Spain, Shehan at Studio des Dahlias in France. Ricardo Camera handled mixing and mastering. The cover artwork is by Shehan. “Babaião” is one of those eight compositions, played live as a trio with Samuel Passos, the Brazilian bassist and composer who has spent the better part of a decade in Barcelona working the city’s Brazilian instrumental music scene, and Pedrinho Augusto, a Brasília-born drummer now also based in Barcelona who trained at Berklee and has played with Gilberto Gil and Victor Wooten among others. Stream and listen to “Babaião” HERE and get your copy of Boas Lembranças HERE The post Daily Discovery: Marcel Vallès Trio – Babaião appeared first on Rhythm Passport.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由西班牙加泰罗尼亚吉他手Marcel Vallès创作，融合了南美三年生活经历带来的巴西、阿根廷和智利音乐元素。作品以吉他与打击乐的二重奏为核心架构，并在现场演出中扩展为三重奏，与巴西低音提琴手Samuel Passos和出生于巴西利亚并在伯克利接受培训的鼓手Pedrinho Augusto合作，属于典型的世界音乐与爵士即兴融合作品。音乐风格偏向传统民谣即兴与拉丁美洲节奏元素，结合了Steve Shehan这位曾与Paul Simon、Bob Dylan合作的资深打击乐手背景，整体呈现跨文化融合特征。从评分维度看，该作品与用户偏好的实验/前卫、学院派爵士、电子和暗潮等风格匹配度较低，更接近世界音乐与爵士融合的中游水准。评论内容较短且近似新闻稿，信息量有限，无法充分评估音乐创新的深度和独特性。

items.body: Miles Davis, born on May 26, 1926 would turn 100 today. The jazz world is rife with memorials of this centennial and since almost anyone who listens to this music has in some way been touched by Davis' music, we at the Free Jazz Blog thought we would pitch in. It is hardly necessary to introduce the iconic trumpeter - you likely own Kind of Blue and Bitches Brew , right? - and while the musical structures on those albums loosened and spawned entire genres themselves, Davis was somewhat ironically ambivalent in his feelings - if not rather dismissive - towards Free-Jazz overall. Oh well, life is complex. To join in the celebration, Free Jazz Blog collaborator Martin Schray proposed that we do what we like to do the most, write about recordings, chosen from Davis' sprawling discography. We did not set rules - no length, no time periods, overlap of albums was fine, just as long as the pieces reflected the writer's feelings towards the recordings. Today, we start off with Martin's reflections and will continue everyday with new impressions from our critics and a few close associates until there is simply no more to say! - Paul Acquaro Miles Davis - Birth of the Cool (Capitol, 1957) In 1949 Capitol signed a contract with the up-and-coming trumpeter Miles Davis for a few singles, which he recorded with his nine-piece band that same and the following year. The first recordings were initially released on 78s, then eight tracks appeared for the first time as an album in 1953, on 10-inch vinyl. Four years later, Capitol released the sessions as an LP with eleven tracks. Even at that early stage of his career, one could already see what would define Miles Davis throughout his musical life: he was an atypical player, yet he possessed remarkable control over timing, dynamics, and emotional impact. The pieces gathered here are precise and focused; they swing with confidence and move between the immediacy of bebop and the sophistication of an Ellington band. Moreover, Davis was a brilliant bandleader who was already able to gather the best musicians around him (here and even more so later on). Birth of the Cool is characterized by the understated elegance of a band that played together perfectly, featuring Gerry Mulligan, Kai Winding, John Lewis, Lee Konitz, and Max Roach (to name just a few). Gil Evans served as arranger and the band’s éminence grise. Ultimately, this album also showcases Davis’s - sometimes underestimated- musical prowess. His mostly vibrato-free tone could be raw, yet also expressive and vulnerable. Just listen to “ Jeru ” and “ Venus de Milo ,” true musical masterpieces. Miles Davis - Kind Of Blue (Columbia, 1959) In various rankings, John Coltrane’s A Love Supreme and Miles Davis’s Kind of Blue are considered the best jazz albums of all time. And yet, especially if it comes to Kind of Blue, connoisseurs of harsher, freer music, don’t listen to this albums that often, because it allegedly has been played to death - just like “ Yesterday ” by the Beatles, “ Smells Like Teen Spirit ” by Nirvana, Antonio Vivaldi’s “ Four Seasons “, Dave Brubeck’s “ Take Five ”, or Keith Jarrett’s “ Köln Concert ”. But does that mean it has lost its quality over time? Not at all! As to Miles Davis, most hard bop players at the time played too much, too long, and too fast. His solution: modal playing instead of frantic chord progressions, mid-tempo, and plenty of space between the notes. He brought only a few sketches to the sessions, yet his choice of ensemble was a compositional masterpiece. The band itself is perhaps the best jazz ensemble that has ever existed: Cannonball Adderley’s blues-soaked, relaxed, deep playing meets John Coltrane’s daring, modal runs; Bill Evans adds impressionistic touches; Paul Chambers’s bass and Jimmy Cobb’s drums are clean, lighthearted, and airy, forming a foundation against which the others have complete freedom. Davis’s trumpet holds the reins. It’s amazing how this sextet of giants swings. If you know “ So What“ , “ Freddie Freeloader “ and “ All Blues “ by heart, give “ Blue in Green “ and “ Flamenco Sketches “ a chance and listen closely. You’ll feel the magic in every note. For the second time at the end of a decade, Davis shifted the course of music in a different direction. At the end of the next decade, he will also determine another change of course. Miles Davis - The Complete In A Silent Way Sessions (Columbia, 1969) The next groundbreaking shift in direction, in the late 1960s, was In A Silent Way. While Columbia’s decision in the late 1990s to release the complete sessions for Davis’s most important albums may have been driven by commercial interests, for Miles’s fans it’s been a welcome opportunity to witness a work in progress. And nowhere is this more evident than on In A Silent Way . At the end of the Sixties Miles Davis was playing in half-empty clubs; soul, funk, and rock musicians were drawing the kind of audience he would have liked to have. For the In A Silent Way sessions between September 1968 and February 1969 he therefore wanted an electric bass and an electric piano. On The Complete Sessions you can literally feel the epochal change in the air. While the first track, “ Mademoiselle Mabry, ” still sounds very much like the old quintet, the change becomes more audible with every new musician. In addition to Chick Corea and Herbie Hancock, Davis brought in Joe Zawinul as the third keyboardist. The core, now formed by three keyboards, and the addition of John McLaughlin as guitarist were the quantum leap that ushered in a new era. Davis wanted simple structures and hip sounds - nothing complex, and above all, no superfluous chords. The result, however, was not jazz-rock, but trippy psychedelic textures that also have an ambient quality. But Davis was also concerned with being at the cutting edge of the times, both in terms of electronic equipment and recording technology. The tried-and-true production techniques no longer made sense to him. Teo Macero played a central role as producer, cutting up the sessions at specific points and reassembling them. As a musical event and group process, what was released back then had never existed before. The fact that the record is nonetheless full of the spirit of spontaneous improvisation is one of the most astonishing events in recent music history. A fun fact regarding the reception of this album is that nearly fifteen minutes of the LP version consist of exact repetitions, and that this went unnoticed and uncommented upon for decades. Miles Davis - Bitches Brew (Columbia, 1970) Six months after In A Silent Way , Miles Davis ultimately broke with the jazz traditionalists. Bitches Brew was even more uncompromising, more radical, more challenging. And it was my first Miles album. I bought it when I was 18; I needed it for a school presentation. When I played it (“ Pharaoh’s Dance“ , fading in somewhere in the middle and then fading out again), most of my classmates were confused. What was that? Jazz or rock or something else entirely? I didn’t understand Bitches Brew back then (and I’m not sure whether I do it today), but I found the sound fascinating. There are few albums I’ve struggled with as much - but it’s been worth it. Davis simply took what he started with In A Silent Way and cranked it up another two notches. As the recording sessions for Bitches Brew approached, he expanded his ensemble once more. Three drum kits, three Fender Rhodes, two bassists, and three percussionists - who infused his music with African and Indian influences - were tasked with blending jazz and rock. He also added Bennie Maupin’s bass clarinet to Wayne Shorter’s sax and John McLaughlin’s guitar. The musical motifs he had devised together with Wayne Shorter twitched like hummingbirds jolted by electricity. The staccato notes from his trumpet ricochet like shrapnels. The collective improvisations collapse like flash floods. Additionally, he led the ensemble like a conductor who has a rough idea of how the music should sound but had to trust his ensemble to make it happen. “ If I heard something in the music that I thought could be expanded, I gave instructions,” Davis says in his biography. The music celebrates the creative process itself; it makes energy palpable. Producer Teo Macero hit the record button the moment Davis stepped into the studio - whenever an amorphous mass of over a dozen instruments coalesced into a collective identity that complemented, repelled, and attracted one another. “ We didn’t talk much during the recording sessions, ” Macero said. “ After the sessions, I spent weeks in the studio, listening to the tapes and beginning to piece the material together. ” The result is structured free improvisation, which allows plenty of room for individuality and often reaches absolute ecstasy, all of which is mercilessly condensed. An album you can listen to forever, one that never bores because it completely transcends boundaries. - Martin Schray Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._cn_summary: 这是一篇Miles Davis经典专辑的乐评，回顾了Birth of the Cool和Kind of Blue两张爵士史上重要作品。文章侧重于历史背景和音乐特质的描述，强调了Miles Davis早期职业生涯的控制力和编排能力，以及他作为乐队领袖的才能。然而，这些专辑属于传统爵士范畴，与用户偏好的实验/前卫音乐及自由即兴方向存在明显差距。评论本身质量尚可，但内容聚焦于已被广泛认可的经典作品，创新性和实验性相对不足。

items.body: Just in time for the World Cup, 4AD has teamed up with New York football-inspired apparel brand Fullkitwnkrs for a new merchandise capsule that reimagines some of the label’s best-known artists and albums through the language of football shirts, supporter scarves, and terrace culture. Full Kit is an independent, self-funded NYC brand founded in 2020, producing football apparel and campaigns for artists. The company has since worked as kitmen for Future Islands, Mount Kimbie, The National, Oneohtrix Point Never, King Krule, and others. The Complicated Opposition collection is available now through the 4AD web store and Bandcamp, with sales running from May 28 through June 8. The capsule features three main pieces: the Cocteau Twins Heaven or Las Vegas Scotland Jersey, the Scott Walker Bish Bosch USA Jersey, and the Colourbox x Air Miami Scarf, which ties into 4AD’s new Complicated Opposition double A-side single, released May 22. Complicated Opposition by Colourbox The Cocteau Twins jersey draws from the colour palette and visual language of the band’s 1990 album Heaven or Las Vegas, while also nodding to the group’s origins in Grangemouth and Scotland’s first World Cup trip in 28 years. The shirt recasts Scottish national team imagery with details pulled from the album’s artwork, including a custom tartan pattern based on the record’s colors and a woven badge featuring the Cocteau Twins’ Lily Dancer logo. Photo by Adam Powell The Scott Walker jersey takes its cues from the Ohio-born artist’s final-era work on Bish Bosch, reworking American soccer design with stark graphics and unusual detailing that mirrors the album’s severe, operatic approach. Photo by Adam Powell Rounding out the capsule is the Colourbox x Air Miami Scarf, a double-sided supporter-style scarf connecting two World Cup-themed tracks from the new Complicated Opposition single: Air Miami’s World Cup Fever and Colourbox’s The Official Colourbox World Cup Theme. The scarf also references the single artwork designed by Chris Bigg, featuring photography by The Douglas Brothers. The scarf will not be sold separately. Instead, it will be produced as a one-of-one item and awarded at random to one customer who purchases a shirt. Photo by Adam Powell As part of the campaign, 4AD will also make a donation to War Child, supporting the organization’s work with children affected by war through education, protection, and advocacy. The 4AD x Full Kit Complicated Opposition capsule is available now through June 8. Shop the collection here. Follow Full Kit: Instagram Website The post 4AD and FULL KIT Announce World Cup Merch Collab Featuring Cocteau Twins, Scott Walker, Colourbox, and Air Miami! appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.body: It features unreleased recordings dating back to 1977 Photo by David Godlis A collection of early unreleased recordings by The Cramps are being packaged together on a new LP, titled Gravest Gravy. Spanning 11 tracks, it features material that the band recorded in 1977 together with producer Alex Chilton of Big Star. The recording sessions ultimately led to the band writing early singles 'Surfin' Bird' and 'Human Fly', as well as other material that was eventually released, but they also worked on a number of other songs that didn't come out. Frontman Lux Interior and guitarist Poison Ivy returned to the material from those sessions in the late 80s hoping to release it, but those plans were shelved for "reasons lost to time", according... The post Lost The Cramps Album, ‘Gravest Gravy’, Set for Release appeared first on The Quietus.

items.excerpt: Due out in July, it's led by new track 'Liars' Photo by Christopher Thomond The Durutti Column are lining up a new album for release this summer. items.body: Review by Hector Enrique — The final stop on Queen's extensive "The Game Tour" world tourn�e between 1980 and 1981 -comprising more than 80 concerts across North America, Europe, South America and Japan- was Montreal, on 24 and 25 November 1981. The band, led by Freddie Mercury, recorded those performances and finally released them in 1984 as "We Will Rock You" on video. Over the years, editing flaws, the ageing of the audio mix and the omission of tracks from the final cut, such as "Flash" and "Hero" -from the "Flash Gordon" soundtrack- prompted the band to remaster the music and restore the film footage. The process culminated in 2007 with the re-release of the work under the title "Rock Montreal".Approximately forty thousand people attended the Montreal Forum over those two nights to see a band in the midst of a musical evolution. Classic tracks such as "Somebody to Love" -featuring a beautiful improvised piano intro by Mercury-, "Killer Queen" and "Now I'm Here" are interwoven with the groovier, pop-infused and more accessible sound that Mercury envisioned for the band in songs such as the futuristic "Play the Game", the rockabilly "Crazy Little Thing Called Love", the funky "Another One Bites the Dust" -both Queen's only number ones on the US Billboard chart- and the world premiere of the single "Under Pressure", co-written with David Bowie.Of course, several of the essential elements of a Queen concert were present: Mercury's banter with the audience during "Now I'm Here"; Brian May's multi-layered guitar work and effects over the backing track of "Brighton Rock"; the tribute to 1950s rock with "Jailhouse Rock"; the intimate moment with the audience during the stripped-back "Love of My Life"; the apotheosis of "Bohemian Rhapsody"; and one of the concert's most delightful surprises, the beautiful "Save Me", led by May on the piano during its introduction.Finally, with the unbeatable and emotional closing medley comprising "We Will Rock You", "We Are the Champions" and the British anthem "God Save the Queen", Queen reaffirmed their superb form and cemented their image as a global supergroup in perfect harmony with a devoted audience.4 stars

items.body: Behzod Abduraimov’s Inferno explores the multifaceted concept of fire, bringing together cornerstones of the piano repertoire by Liszt, Debussy, and Stravinsky alongside a lesser-known offering by Carl Czerny. Inferno Amazon Presto Apple Because Czerny is typically associated with the practice room rather than the concert hall, Abduraimov’s decision to include the Op. 33 Variations on a Theme by Rode is particularly intriguing. Any initial misgivings are quickly dispelled by a charming performance of this rare gem. Here, the inferno manifests as acrobatic fireworks; the pianist revels in each leap, turn, and twist with enviable agility. Capturing the work’s inherently carefree nature, he evidently relishes the technical display. While the album’s conceptual arc takes a decisive turn toward the dramatic with Liszt‘s Dante Sonata, Abduraimov navigates this transition sensibly. Bravado is naturally infused throughout the writing, yet the prevailing strength of this interpretation lies in its profound balance. Even in the most dazzling passages, or those fraught with tension, the pianist treats notes and phrases with meticulous care. Accents and fortes are never driven to harshness, and the most fleeting lines remain thoughtfully contoured. When the score demands power, he marshals the recurring textural and motivic elements to devastating effect. His interlocking octave glissandos possess a chilling sharpness, the dotted rhythms are articulated with unyielding resolve, and those treacherous tremolos unleash a fury that vividly evokes the underworld. Debussy’s Suite Bergamasque presents an entirely different interpretation of the inferno. Frankly, it is the one inclusion whose relationship to the overarching theme feels somewhat tenuous. This conceptual disconnect aside, it remains a welcome addition, offering a comforting contrast to the intensity of Liszt and Stravinsky. Effectively demonstrating his versatility, Abduraimov proves he can be as musically affable as he is fierce. Opening the cycle, the Prelude is undeniably charming, though it could perhaps benefit from slightly more emphasis and demarcation in certain structural moments. Nevertheless, this lighthearted approach succeeds wonderfully in the quieter passages, illuminating the delicacy of Debussy’s textural language. Carrying a similar carefree spirit, the Menuet benefits from Abduraimov’s acute responsiveness to harmonic shifts, which injects a perfect measure of whimsy. At the heart of the suite, Clair de lune certainly does not disappoint. Maintaining the fluidity established in preceding movements, the performer achieves a breathtaking atmosphere of quiet contemplation. Particularly notable is the passage beginning near the one-minute mark, an interpretive highlight that offers exquisite shades of piano and a soothing resonance demanding to be fully savored. Stravinsky’s Petroushka marks a return to unbridled extroversion, with the first two movements deserving high praise for their superb execution. Although the Danse Russe may not be as relentlessly heady or pointillistic as benchmark readings by Alexis Weissenberg or Maurizio Pollini, Abduraimov’s distinct strength lies in his seamless blending of harmonies and chords, granting the piano a remarkably orchestral profile. Evoking the visual elements of the original ballet, his leaps and flourishes possess an infectious playfulness. Moving forward, Chez Petroushka serves as an exquisite study in detail: every note sounds as clear as a bell, and each phrase contributes to a vivid tableau of impishness, suspense, and disquiet. Behzod Abduraimov. Brahms‘s Op. 119 No. 1 Intermezzo rounds out the program on a deeply nuanced, wistful note. In this closing piece, the inferno’s intensity morphs into a slow, nostalgic burn, its inherent tenderness and longing conveyed with profound sensitivity and beauty. One minor grievance arises not from the performance or the superb sound engineering, but rather from the liner notes. Curiously, the overarching theme is never actively explored in any of the accompanying descriptions of the selections. Such a discussion is something many listeners would find highly insightful, and it could easily have been addressed through an interview with the performer. Alternatively, perhaps the underlying intent of the album is to encourage listeners to forge their own perspectives on what constitutes an inferno. To that end, Abduraimov’s magnificent performances provide an undeniably compelling catalyst.
